title: Forget petrodollars, ‘chip-dollars’ show U.S. power now flows from tech dominance—but the new currency regime is ‘inherently riskier,’ analyst says
summary: "The potent combination of US control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in US allies has given the US enormous control over chips."
content: Semiconductors are surpassing oil as the linchpin of the dollar’s global reach, demonstrating U.S. technological might but also revealing a less stable foundation, according to Deutsche Bank . In a note last week, foreign exchange strategist Mallika Sachdeva pointed out that for the first time in modern history, global trade in chips now exceeds trade in oil and gas. Excluding China, Asia’s surplus in the chip trade matches petroleum-related surpluses in the Persian Gulf, she added. That’s as AI hyperscalers keep ramping up capital expenditures, which are expected to top $1 trillion next year, further propping up chip trade flows. “The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of U.S. power — from geopolitical to technological leadership,” Sachdeva wrote, adding that the so-called petrodollar is quickly being superseded by the new “chip-dollar.” The petrodollar regime goes back to a deal struck in 1974 when Saudi Arabia agreed to price its oil in dollars and invest surpluses in U.S. assets, especially Treasury debt. In return, the American military ensured security in the region and free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. And because oil is a core input to global manufacturing and transport, supply chains have a natural incentive to dollarize. Indeed, Mideast oil and gas are used to make petrochemicals, fertilizer, and even helium. But the underpinnings of the petrodollar are breaking down due to the Iran war as Tehran exposes the limits of the U.S. military, while the AI boom is sending a tsunami of capital from Asia to the U.S. This time around, rather than Mideast kingdoms recycling oil-trade surpluses into U.S. debt, Asia’s chip behemoths are recycling chip-trade surpluses into U.S. stocks. In fact, South Korean households have 90% of their equity exposure in the U.S., according to Deutsche Bank. Overall, foreign purchases of U.S. equities are now more than double that of Treasuries. “The emerging chip-dollar regime is one where US technology leadership is motivating global savings to be reinvested in U.S. companies — providing funding for the US corporate sector to make enormous investments in new technology such as AI,” Sachdeva explained. Chip dominance begets dollar dominance Just like how oil penetrated industrial supply chain, chips are embedded in the digital economy as inputs in consumer electronics, automobiles, computers, communication devices, and AI systems. She estimated chips account for more than 50% of the capex for a data center. And despite Asia’s dominance in chipmaking, 70% of the industry’s profits flow to U.S. firms. In addition, the key countries in the supply chain of advanced chips are friendly with Washington, namely Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. “The potent combination of U.S. control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in U.S. allies has given the U.S. enormous control over chips,” Sachdeva added. At the same time, chips ensure continued dollar dominance in global trade, payments, capital markets, and private sector savings, while also supporting America’s AI buildout, she pointed out. But Deutsche Bank cautioned that the new currency regime has a “circularity” risk because capital flowing from Asian chip hotspots provides financing to U.S. companies driving the AI boom. That means if consumer demand for compute can’t support AI investments, earnings for tech companies would come down—as well as chip demand. The focus on stocks over debt means more instability too. U.S. stocks overall are three times as volatile as Treasuries—and tech stocks are up to 10 times as much, Sachdeva noted. “A dollar driven by chips, AI and private capital connections should be inherently riskier,” she warned. That risk was on display in recent weeks as tech stocks sold off sharply on fears the AI boom was about to go bust. And although Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday sparked a big rebound, the Trump administration is cracking down on foreign access to U.S. AI technology, potentially curbing the chip trade. Dollar vs. yuan — Coke vs. Pepsi To be sure, threats to the dollar’s status as the global reserve currency have come and gone over the decades. More recently, the proliferation of U.S. financial sanctions has given countries more reason to diversify away from the dollar. But no credible alternatives have emerged yet, despite China’s aggressive efforts to internationalize the yuan. China facilitates its use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets. Beijing also promotes “China prices,” or yuan benchmarks on domestic commodity exchanges. Chinese banks have more than doubled their yuan lending to overseas borrowers since 2023, and the central bank has reached currency swap agreements with dozens of peers. But Zongyuan Zoe Liu, senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relation, argued in Foreign Affairs last month that Beijing doesn’t actually want to replace the dollar on the world stage. “Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy,” she wrote. “From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
summary: Rather than paying for the most powerful AI model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work.
content: As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency. “ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.” Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through cloud platform Vercel went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year. “Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance. The case for ‘good enough’ AI Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice. In 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2 , citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving users access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves. In the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models. “For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday , a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says. “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.” Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform . “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.) Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant : an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for users based on their individual aesthetic preferences. “[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim. A hybrid approach Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models. Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia , a Singapore-based wellness clinic, says he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says. He compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he says. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.” Token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones. “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” says Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.” Harder choices Yet a company’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba , and z.AI ; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology. “The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement . On Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models , in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing new restrictions that might anger Beijing. In a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote. Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported . “For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.” A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return . The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, says Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU). “Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he says. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.” Still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance ,” says Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.” For businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Lori Huang’s Nvidia-funded foundation gained about $2.3 billion in a day on Jensen Huang’s return
summary: Most of the foundation's payouts go to a donor-advised fund, and its mandatory giving is set to climb as the stake grows.
content: When Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, shareholders weren’t the only winners. The Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, the private charity run by Huang’s wife, Lori, holds roughly 59 million Nvidia shares, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement. Nvidia stock jumped more than 30% to close at $165.05, Fortune reported . At that price, the foundation’s stake was worth about $9.7 billion, roughly $2.3 billion more than it was worth at Friday’s close. Huang told cheering employees at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters that he would be “a better CEO the second time around.” Wall Street seemed to agree: The S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. An 11-day round trip The rally erased much of the damage from Huang’s resignation, announced Nov. 12 . He stepped down after admitting to an affair and amid reports linking him to Alice Huang (no relation), a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials concluded was passing information to China, as well as a reported affair with a direct report. Chinese officials called the spying claims a fabrication. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14.35% in intraday trading that day before closing down 4.34%. A comeback campaign took shape almost immediately. An open letter started by an Nvidia employee had more than 206,000 names by Monday, including Elon Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. President Trump publicly urged the board to bring Huang back and called the board as it deliberated. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told The New York Times ’ Andrew Ross Sorkin at the paper’s DealBook summit. Who runs the Huang foundation Lori Huang has been the foundation’s president since 2014, with Jensen as secretary and chief financial officer, Fortune reported this month . She is also co-trustee of the trusts that hold most of the couple’s Nvidia stake, the bulk of a fortune Forbes valued at about $144 billion at Monday’s close. The couple met at Oregon State University. Jensen cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, and the company now ranks No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . It was the most valuable company on the list when it was published in June. The Huangs started the foundation in 2007 with 370,000 Nvidia shares worth $12.6 million at the time. Its assets climbed from $828 million at the end of 2020 to $9.2 billion at the end of 2024, according to its tax filings . Last year, data firm FoundationMark ranked it among the 15 largest private foundations in the U.S., alongside the Rockefeller Foundation and the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation. “Big philanthropy now is tech-driven, like many other things, far more than it used to be,” FoundationMark CEO John Seitz told CNBC at the time. For its size, the foundation keeps a remarkably low profile. It has no website, and as of 2023 it reported no paid staff. The Huangs keep adding to it. In June 2025, their living trust gave the foundation 440,000 Nvidia shares, worth about $60 million, and half as many to a donor-advised fund, according to an SEC filing CNBC cited. Where the money goes The couple’s public gifts have grown. They gave $50 million to Oregon State in 2022 and $22.5 million to California College of the Arts in 2025, and last November they committed $5 million a year to the San Francisco Opera. In July, they gave $75 million to Vanderbilt University for a new art, architecture, and design college in San Francisco. “I don’t give anything away,” Huang told Stanford Engineering in 2010, after the couple funded the school’s Jen-Hsun Huang Engineering Center. Later in the same interview, he said: “The way I think about it is I’m investing in the next generation, to help us and to inspire us to create even better and more useful technologies.” Most of the foundation’s payouts, though, go to a donor-advised fund . In 2024, $82 million of its $126 million payout, about two-thirds, went to DAFgiving360, the sponsor formerly known as Schwab Charitable, Inside Philanthropy reported . The year before, a $46 million gift to a Schwab DAF made up 77% of its disbursements, according to CNBC. DAFs give donors an immediate tax deduction. Unlike private foundations, they don’t have to distribute on a set schedule or disclose where the money goes. That matters more as the foundation grows. Private foundations must distribute at least 5% of their assets each year, based on the prior year’s average value, and FoundationMark estimated the Huang foundation had to pay out $369 million in 2025, nearly triple its 2024 total. The same stock that powered Monday’s gain also concentrates the foundation’s risk. Nvidia still faces an internal investigation into Huang, a reported SEC probe into whether its disclosures misled investors, and a subpoena from California’s attorney general. “You’re basically going to Vegas and you’re betting on black or red,” Doug Macauley, a partner at Cambridge Associates, told CNBC last year about foundations that hold a concentrated position in a single company. On Monday, the wheel landed the Huangs’ way. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘Paid parental leave is no longer a nice-to-have’: New dads now take paid leave more often than new moms
summary: Fathers are also three times as likely as mothers to spend vacation days on a newborn, a KPMG analysis of Census data finds.
content: You’re told to enjoy all the moments, good and bad, with your newborn because, sooner than later, you’ll blink and they’ll be adults shipping off to college and bringing back kids of their own. Unfortunately, feeding a growing baby now means trading those fleeting moments for labor hours, and rarely does a job’s parental leave policy include a special clause for “18 years of watching them grow up.” Those lucky enough to have parents or other relatives who can look after their newborns can rely on them for a bit, while others who can afford it hire nannies and live-in help. The rest, reliant on dual-income households, opt to stagger their parental leave. Until recently, only the mom took time off from work. For births before 1986, a first-time mother was more than three times as likely as a first-time father to take paid time off after the baby arrived. That gap has now flipped: from 2021 to 2025, 56.1% of first-time fathers took some form of paid leave in the 12 weeks after a birth, slightly more than the 52.5% of first-time mothers, according to a new KPMG Economics analysis of Census data . For births before 1986, just 11.5% of fathers took paid leave. But now, counting unpaid time off, nearly three in four first-time fathers take leave after a birth, more than five times the 13.7% who did before 1986. The biggest jump came for births in the late 2010s, as states expanded paid leave programs and more employers began offering it as a benefit. For companies, the shift affects how they design leave policies, plan staffing and keep workers. Paid vs. unpaid leave The growth is specifically in paid parental leave. For births from 2019 to 2025, 53.1% of first-time fathers used it, up from 39.5% for births from 2011 to 2018. Over the same period, fathers’ use of paid vacation time ticked down, which suggests dads are swapping vacation days for parental leave. Many still lean on vacation time. Fathers were three times as likely as mothers to use paid vacation after a birth, 23.2% vs. 7.3%, which may be because they don’t have access to the disability leave many mothers use. Nestler writes that this keeps a paycheck coming but leaves less vacation for actual vacation, which can wear on employee satisfaction and lead to burnout. Mothers, meanwhile, were nearly twice as likely as fathers to take unpaid parental leave, 33.6% vs. 17.8%. Their share taking any paid leave has grown more slowly, up 15.1 percentage points since before 1986 compared with 44.6 points for fathers, partly because mothers started from a higher base. The same trend shows up in state data. The U.S. has no federal paid family leave law, but 14 states and Washington, D.C., have passed their own programs . Maine, which passed its program in 2023 , began paying benefits of up to 12 weeks in May. In California, which offers up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave, men filed 51% of bonding claims in 2025 , the first time they outnumbered women in the program’s history. When the program started in 2004, men filed about 18% of claims. Men have also overtaken women in Colorado and Washington , according to Paid Leave for All, The KPMG figures cover a specific group: parents who worked during the pregnancy and took leave in the 12 weeks after the birth. That is a different group from men who leave the workforce to stay home, which falls under the long-term decline in men’s labor force participation. A forthcoming KPMG analysis of the same data will examine how long new parents stayed out before returning to work. Access is still uneven. Among workers with paid leave, more than one in five couldn’t use it to care for a child or an aging relative, according to the analysis, and lower-income workers are less able to afford unpaid time off. Paid paternity leave and flexible schedules are largely available only to dads with good jobs , and low-wage fathers often avoid taking leave because they can’t afford to lose income. Even where a state benefit exists, many fathers leave it on the table: One study found that New York dads forgo $1.6 billion in paid state leave. Nestler said employers should treat the trend as a hiring and retention issue. “The workforce has changed and what workers expect from employers has also changed. That is especially the case with caregiving and paid leave benefits,” he said to Fortune in a statement. “Facing a demographic crunch—aging population that is retiring along with a more restrictive immigration policy—employers need to compete for top talent.” “Paid parental leave is no longer a nice-to-have HR benefit; it is a core workforce and business investment that can help improve satisfaction, retention and productivity of a key employee segment: new parents, mainly Millennials and Gen Z, many of whom are managers, directors and leaders.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘Look what I’ve produced’: Inside ‘peacock parenting,’ where kids become their parents’ status symbols
summary: Parents say they're more affectionate than their own parents were. But when a child's milestone exists mainly to impress an audience, experts say kids pay the price.
content: Today’s parents are consciously trying to break with how they were raised, prioritizing emotional well-being over punitive discipline. But a parenting phenomenon gaining attention seems at odds with that generational shift : “peacock parenting,” in which children become status symbols for their parents. In ZERO TO THREE’s First Voice survey of more than 2,200 parents of children ages 5 and under, conducted this summer, 61% say they tell their kids “I love you” more often than their own parents did. Sixty percent say they focus more on their children’s mental health, and 56% say they won’t use the physical discipline they experienced growing up. Peacock parenting describes a pattern of narcissistic behavior in which parents prioritize their own need for admiration and control over their children’s emotional needs. There’s no prevalence data specific to the term, and the underlying psychology is not new. What has changed is the public visibility of children’s lives, and the opportunities for parents to turn their kids’ achievements into social and financial capital. Parenting has a new report card “Pride says, ‘I’m so happy for you.’ Peacocking says, ‘look what I’ve produced,’” says Dr. Christine Ghilain, a double board-certified clinical neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Health Neuropsychology in New Jersey. “It tips over when the moment is for the audience and not the child.” She says the red flags include an achievement that doesn’t feel real until it’s been posted, moments staged or redone for the camera, repeated posting even after a child objects, and a parent’s mood that rises and falls with the likes. The desire for an audience may have as much to do with insecurity as vanity. In the First Voice survey, 53% of parents said raising a child is harder than they expected. And 42% said managing their own mental health had been a challenge in the past month. Ghilain believes the pressures and isolation of modern parenthood help explain why parents seek validation through their children. “Parenting has no report card, so a child’s achievements or cuteness can feel like proof we’re doing it right, and an audience’s reaction can feel like a grade,” she says. Tara Oporto, a mother of five who has shared her children’s accomplishments on Facebook for years, wonders whether family size and gender also play a role. She raised a stepson and twin boys, all the same age, alongside two younger daughters. “When you have three boys hitting milestones at the same time, there are too many of them to make any one of their accomplishments about you,” she says. Oporto suspects parents may identify more closely with the achievements of children of the same gender. A former singer herself, she recognized that impulse when her older daughter made it into her university’s top a cappella group. “When it’s something that’s actually in line with the parent’s own unique talents, you get double duty: you’re proud of the child, but you’re also identifying your own wins and passions through what they’re doing.” And it’s not just happening online (or with mothers). “We see this so often in sports with ‘daddyball,’ where dad coaches live vicariously through their kids on the field,” says Dr. David Timpanaro, founder and CEO of Step Up Family Services, a New Jersey behavioral health provider. He points to fathers who coach their own children’s teams and hand them the most coveted positions. Kids pushed to meet their parents’ expectations in sports tend to quit earlier, he adds. National data points the same way. In a survey of nearly 4,000 kids ages 10 to 17 by the Aspen Institute’s Project Play , 21% of former players said they had been pressured to play when they didn’t want to, compared with 9% of kids still playing. The business of looking like a good parent Unlike “sharenting,” the practice of sharing children’s lives online , peacock parenting is distinguished by its motivations. “It tips into peacock parenting when the child’s moment is used to impress an audience, or when the parent needs the display more than the child needs the celebration,” says Colleen Souza, a mother of three and former classroom teacher. “Peacock parenting uses the child as proof of the parent’s worth. It’s growing now because comparison comes at kids and adults 24/7, and the feed rewards whoever puts on the best show.” There are financial incentives, too. A 2025 study published in PLOS One analyzed more than 5,000 Instagram posts from 10 British motherhood influencers and found children in nearly three-quarters of them. Of the posts featuring children, 46% contained sponsorships or product advertising. “The parent gets a quick hit of status, but the platforms and brands built on display profit most,” Souza says. Lawmakers have started to follow the money. Illinois became the first state to require parents to set aside earnings for child influencers, under a law that took effect in July 2024 , and California and Minnesota have since passed their own versions. What children stand to lose Lenore Skenazy, president of Let Grow and author of Free-Range Kids , sees a disconnect between what society rewards and what children actually need. Skenazy argues that society overvalues, rewards, and perfects what children biologically need: opportunities to do things for fun, out of curiosity, or to take a little risk. By giving children those experiences and plenty of affection, she says, parents can feel secure in their parenting without needing social media validation, likes or hearts. For a generation determined to break with the way they were raised, the challenge may be separating the desire to be good parents from the desire to be seen as good parents. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: They were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and in college when their friends got accused of cheating. Now their AI software polices 40 colleges
summary: Four Purdue students built Syntax, which records how an essay gets written. Teachers get the evidence. Students can buy it for $9.99.
content: When OpenAI released ChatGPT on Nov. 30, 2022, Derin Suzener was a high school senior already leaning toward a career in AI. He got there “without having taken a single computer science course back in 11th grade,” he told Fortune . “I did not start using ChatGPT until I entered university, actually.” Nikita Kravcenko, his future cofounder, was also in high school, taking AP classes where “my teachers were bombarding students with anti-AI policy, because it was like a new technology at that point,” he said. “So they were very fearful of what it could do and write. So they were essentially having a craze over it.” By the time they got to Purdue, the craze had casualties. “I was seeing all of my friends get accused of cheating with AI on their computer science assignments,” Suzener said. “And they would have a pretty hard time proving it, actually.” So Suzener, Kravcenko and two classmates built a way to prove it. Their company, Remora, makes Syntax, a document editor that records how a student writes a paper (typing speed, cursor movement, what gets pasted in) and flags anything odd for the teacher to review. The founders say it’s used in classrooms at 40 U.S. colleges and universities, though they declined to name any, saying that identifying customers could help larger competitors go after the same schools. The company says four more institutions will start using it next semester. Students can also buy it themselves, starting at $9.99 for three months. The pitch is protection for students who did their own work. “The guilty are truly proven to be guilty, and then the innocent are exonerated,” Kravcenko said. The fear is common. In a YouGov poll of 2,373 UK students, commissioned by the student-support company Studiosity, 52% named “being accused of cheating when I did nothing wrong” as one of the things stressing them out, Times Higher Education reported in February. Kravcenko, the company’s CFO, is a third-year finance and accounting student at Purdue’s Daniels School of Business who oversees finances and outreach. Suzener, the CEO, is a senior studying computer science, AI and philosophy. He oversees product, engineering, strategy and research, along with the analysis algorithms, and is spending this semester on exchange at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden. Their cofounders are CTO Robert Juliano, a Purdue junior studying cybersecurity, network engineering and forensic science; and Nicholas Ball, the chief information security officer, a recent Purdue cybersecurity graduate now in the university’s master’s program. The four came up with the idea in the spring 2025 semester and founded the company that June. Courtesy of Remora Called into a meeting Suzener remembers one friend in particular from his first year. The friend was accused of cheating on a coding assignment and called into a half-hour meeting to explain his code. “He studied hours for it just to be able to explain it perfectly,” Suzener said. “He was really stressed about it.” He passed, because he had written the code himself. The stress lasted longer than the meeting. In Suzener’s philosophy classes, detectors were flagging essays because they read like machine output. “But an AI and a person can arrive at the exact same sentence by some given probability,” he said. While testing Syntax in Purdue courses, the founders met a student who, Kravcenko said, “was embroiled in an academic dishonesty hearing for the majority of the year.” To clear himself, the student had to produce “Google Docs history documents, actual time receipts,” Kravcenko said. The student told the founders Syntax would have taken much of that pressure off him. The founders started with Turnitin, the plagiarism checker most students know from high school. Kravcenko said its AI scoring, which reads only the finished text, produced false positives. “Why not make something that can portray the entire picture of how the work was written instead of just diluting it into a score?” The blank page Suzener explains Syntax the way he explains it to teachers. “When you open a document for the first time, like Google Docs, you have a blank page. And as a student, you will start writing things. And maybe this is just the brainstorming phase. Maybe you’re just taking notes. Maybe you write a whole paragraph in one sitting. It’s completely possible and this changes based on who you are, how you write.” Text-based detectors like GPTZero, Suzener said, train models on human and machine writing and score the finished product. Syntax skips the prose. “We don’t actually look at the text that’s being written,” Suzener said. “We look instead to the entire behavioral process that took place to actually arrive at that final text.” He compares it to a CAPTCHA, which cares less about whether you clicked the right traffic lights than about how your cursor got there. Syntax logs typing speed, typing behavior and cursor movement inside its own editor. From that, Suzener says, it can tell a human from a script and see how a student pastes and cites. It can also catch something subtler. “Are you typing something while looking at something else completely at a steady pace? Which is obviously not a great sign of your own work being done.” Syntax flags those patterns, and the teacher decides what they mean. “A lot of AI detectors have the final product only,” Kravcenko said. “We have access to the entire writing process from start to finish.” Suzener described a case where an instructor at a California university got a flag on a student’s paper, called the student in and went through Syntax’s record. The student had pasted in material from an outside document and cited none of it. That was sloppy, not AI. Suzener recalled the teacher writing back, “great job, guys. Thank you for making it very clear.” Teachers also get GraderAid, a grading tool built on Bloom’s Taxonomy, a framework educators use to gauge how deeply a student understands material. It checks a submission against the instructor’s own course objectives. The company says GraderAid doesn’t use large language models, and the teacher makes the final call. Who pays Students can buy access directly: $9.99 for three months, $14.99 for six and $19.99 for nine, with a seven-day free trial. Instructors can cover a whole class, and schools can license Syntax through their learning-management systems, with setup for Canvas and Brightspace. Both are priced case by case. In other words, a student who’s afraid of being accused can pay for their own alibi. The pilots were free. Then the company started charging, and “we’ve actually started making enough to compensate for the cost of actually hosting the service,” Kravcenko said. Remora started charging subscriptions in September, and that revenue has covered its operating costs since, Kravcenko said in an email. The company reached operating break-even in October and is still self-funded. The founders declined to disclose revenue or the number of paying users. They priced it as students, Kravcenko said: “we, as students, know what teachers want to pay, we know what students would like to pay.” The founders count GPTZero and Turnitin as the incumbents. They hadn’t heard of Pangram, a newer detector, when they started. “Pangram has only recently become sort of like a bigger deal across academic circles,” Suzener said. A much bigger company already sells something similar. Grammarly’s Authorship feature, rolled out widely in October 2024, logs what a student types and pastes and can replay how a document was made. Grammarly offers it on its free tier and pitches it the same way, to “a student seeking to protect yourself against accusations of plagiarism,” according to the company . Kravcenko said in an email that Authorship documents a single document’s history, while Syntax “takes a longitudinal approach, building a behavioral fingerprint across a student’s submissions.” It learns how a student normally writes, he said, and flags when a paper departs from that. Teachers have responded warmly, the founders say. One instructor emailed to say they had been needing a tool like this and had recommended it to colleagues in other departments. Another sent long feedback describing Syntax as a “friendly neighborhood watch” that left students less inclined to cheat. The founders say they also saw more engagement with the material in that class. Being watched Asked whether students had pushed back, Kravcenko said not “directly from students.” He suspects the ones who object keep quiet. “They will just try to find a way to cheat.” Suzener expects some resentment. “We sort of know students, and we know how they will react to things,” he said. When a teacher runs every paper through GPTZero, “the students will generally not be happy.” Syntax is trying to do better “by trying to bring transparency,” he said, “but there will obviously be some discontent, and that’s not very easy to stop.” In a follow-up, the company said it actively welcomes student feedback and that Syntax is designed to rebuild the trust students have lost in today’s AI detectors. It says it records behavior only inside its own editor, doesn’t sell student data or use it for advertising, lets students keep ownership of their work and doesn’t use that work to train AI models. When teachers ask whether Syntax is a policing tool, Kravcenko said, “the answer is no.” Critics of process tracking have two objections: the privacy of the draft, and how easy the tracking is to beat. “I feel entirely naked just describing how I write—I would be mortified if someone could see that entire process,” Marc Watkins, a faculty member who writes about AI in education, wrote in a 2025 post on Grammarly’s tool. He added: “Simply opening a new tab and manually copying an AI output via typing or automating the task will defeat it.” That steady retyping is the pattern Suzener says Syntax is built to catch. The founders aren’t anti-AI. Kravcenko said a mentor of his uses AI to role-play emails and presentations, which he thinks is how it should be used: “having, like, a partner that is sitting on your shoulder instead of at the keyboard writing for you is very helpful.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Sam Altman needs Jony Ive to create a physical AI device because Apple will never give OpenAI the real-world data ChatGPT needs, Tony Fadell says
summary: Former Apple executive Tony Fadell says privacy rules stop OpenAI from reading context data on the iPhone. A companion gadget would let it collect that data itself.
content: Sam Altman asked former Apple design chief Jony Ive to create a physical device for OpenAI because the AI company cannot get the data it needs from the iPhones it runs on, Tony Fadell says. Fadell worked with Ive at Apple and is best known for being the “father of the iPod” and a co-creator of the iPhone. He founded Build Collective and previously founded Nest Labs. Fadell spoke to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon. AI evidently works well for text, images, and video on the flat screens of our phones and laptops. So it is not obvious what an OpenAI consumer device would look like, or even do, given that ChatGPT can already function on any computing device you own. We know only that OpenAI hopes it will usurp the iPhone as the world’s most popular consumer electronics product. The reason OpenAI is going to such lengths, Fadell believes, is because it needs data about the physical world that Apple refuses to give it due to privacy concerns. “They have to build products because they cannot get contextual information out of the phone,” Fadell said. “So what they have to do is they have to recreate the GPS, the microphones, the speakers, the cameras, the temperature, you name it. Like, all kinds of different things that they have to get, because Apple will not allow you to get that out of the phone.” “It’s really to get around all the restrictions because of all the privacy things for Apple. That’s why,” he said. “The more context that you have for AI, the better the answers, and the more quickly [you] can get to them.” “Apple has all the products with all the context in your home, but you’re not going to get that data. Apple’s not going to give you that because of the privacy restrictions,” he said. The need for “edge” computing At some point OpenAI will want to move parts of the processing function behind ChatGPT out from its own cloud servers and onto your devices, so-called “edge computing.” For many simple tasks, AI does not need an array of servers to deliver answers to prompts. The processing power in your laptop or on your phone will do. But it might be difficult for OpenAI to persuade Apple to allow its vast network of iOS and macOS devices to run OpenAI tasks. “So they also want to move processing to the edge, but they don’t get access to all that [from Apple]. So what they’re doing is they’ll make a companion device that’s basically a stripped-out smartphone without a screen on it, with all the sensors and everything, and then they just pipe it through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth back up to the network through your phone, back up to AI agents that could be running on the cloud, or maybe in an app on your phone.” What physical form will the device take? Fadell speculates: “So you’ve heard they’re gonna make a phone, they’re gonna make a pendant. They’re going to make a pen. They’re going to make a speaker because they’re just trying to get context.” OpenAI was approached for comment. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘Businesses hate chaos’: $166 billion in tariff refunds are flowing to companies, not the customers who paid
summary: TJX, Acushnet and Stanley Black & Decker are steering part of their refunds to bonuses. A trade lawyer says consumers who paid higher prices have little legal recourse.
content: American companies are collecting roughly $166 billion in tariff refunds, plus interest, for costs that many consumers helped pay. Some of that money is going to bonuses. At least nine public companies have disclosed using part of their refunds for executive or employee bonuses, according to a ProPublica investigation that used an AI tool to analyze securities filings and earnings calls. They include TJX , the owner of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls; Acushnet, which owns the golf brand Titleist; and the toolmaker Stanley Black & Decker. TJX has set aside $167 million of its $463 million in refunds for incentive pay and discretionary bonuses for non-executive associates, according to its third-quarter earnings release , as Fortune reported last week . That is about 3% of the $5.5 billion TJX earned in its last fiscal year. Acushnet disclosed that about $12 million of its $45.8 million in refunds would go to incentive compensation. Stanley Black & Decker, which is getting at least $298 million according to ProPublica’s refund database , hasn’t said how much will fund bonuses. The money is landing with importers rather than the customers who absorbed higher prices, and few precedents exist for a scale like this. “I think it’s fair to say that at this scale, it’s unprecedented, partly because the scale of business right now is unlike what we’ve seen in prior years,” Kathleen Claussen, a law professor at Georgetown University, told Fortune . How emergency tariffs turned into a refund windfall In February 2025, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming into the country and announced tariffs on Mexico, Canada and China, the countries he blamed. About two months later, he declared a second emergency over the U.S. trade deficit and unveiled tariffs on nearly every U.S. trading partner. Both rounds relied on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, which lets the president regulate international commerce during a national emergency. “Everyone told me that it was very difficult keeping up with the speed and complexity of change… and what exactly that meant for their companies,” Jonathan Todd, a partner at the law firm Benesch, told Fortune . Todd said some companies set up war rooms dedicated to tariffs, while others built new compliance programs and policies. “It’s just created chaos, and businesses hate chaos,” Adams Lee, an international trade lawyer at Harris Sliwoski, told Fortune . Lee said many companies worked with manufacturers and suppliers to share the costs or strike deals. On Feb. 20, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that IEEPA does not give the president power to impose tariffs, ending them. U.S. Customs and Border Protection had disbursed more than $115 billion in refunds as of August . Do shoppers have any claim to the money? By late July, shoppers had filed more than 100 proposed class actions seeking a share of the refunds, according to an analysis by the law firm Thompson Coburn . Companies facing suits include Walmart , Target , Nike and Lululemon . Many companies that sell to other businesses have been sharing refunds with those clients. Regular consumers may be out of luck. “Unless there was something that was in the contract terms and the sales terms at the time that the tariffs were first imposed,” Lee said. “It’s really difficult to say that there was a legal obligation for any refunds, unexpected refunds, to be paid back to any of the downstream customers.” Some companies are compensating customers anyway. UPS and FedEx have set up portals for customers to claim refunds. Burlington Stores , which received roughly $55 million, has said it will use the money to return value to customers and told ProPublica none of it would go to bonuses. “We’re telling the importers, look, your customers may not necessarily have that strong of a legal claim to say they’re entitled to some share of your refunds, but they are your customers, right?” Lee said. “If you want to keep your customers happy, what are you going to do?” Mark Marinaro, a Titleist customer, said that after hearing about the ProPublica investigation, his faith in the company was at an “all-time low.” “I’m all for staff getting bonuses, but it should come out of their already healthy margins, not out of a refund for tariffs that have been ruled unlawful,” Marinaro wrote in an email to Fortune . More refunds, and more tariffs, may be coming The pressure on companies could grow now that Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, said Emily Gershon, the founder of Parapet Advisors and a former international trade specialist at the International Trade Administration. In February, Senators Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Peter Welch pressed Trump for a plan to refund consumers and small businesses. “I think that we are going to see a lot of mounting political pressure on companies to return money to consumers, even if not directly doing so, in ways that reduce prices moving forward,” Gershon told Fortune . Tariffs haven’t gone away. After the ruling, Trump imposed a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which the Court of International Trade ruled unlawful in May; the government’s appeal is pending. When it expired in July , new Section 301 tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 economies replaced it. Both can be challenged in court. The Court of International Trade also certified a nationwide class action in October covering importers that paid IEEPA tariffs but haven’t filed their own suits, a potential path to full refunds for thousands of smaller businesses. “There could be refunds in the future beyond even what you’re seeing today, and there will also be increased tariff burden for the near term,” Todd said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Thanksgiving as we know it was dreamed up by a women’s magazine editor who lobbied 5 presidents — Lincoln finally bit during the Civil War
summary: Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey’s Lady’s Book, petitioned five presidents before Abraham Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday.
content: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence. Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys. The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving ” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it. Creating today’s Thanksgiving The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts . On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other. The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book , which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War. Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family. She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck , Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving , along with instructions for what the day could look like. Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business , making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious. Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories – and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving. Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War. Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door , collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops. The holiday caught on gradually . Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated. Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier. Assimilating immigrants Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants. This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast . “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey. The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery. Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American. But many Americans believed they could – although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation. In the early 20th century, public schools taught about Thanksgiving and sent children home with recipe cards so that their parents could cook the same kinds of recipes Hale had popularized in the previous century. Schools framed the Pilgrims and their first Thanksgiving as the spiritual, if not literal, ancestors of all Americans: the first “immigrants.” They didn’t dwell on how the Pilgrims’ arrival looked more like colonization than immigration. The holiday became a way to include newcomers in the national myth. By the 1920s, in fact, Thanksgiving was the most celebrated holiday in public schools . Pleck quotes one Jewish immigrant reflecting on his childhood and saying the Pilgrims were a way to connect “us offspring of Jewish immigrants – our own exiled fathers who had crossed the seas – and the traditions of Protestant America .” Students acted out the first Thanksgiving and were told they belonged to a “nation of immigrants.” While some immigrant parents rejected the holiday, others embraced it, with spins to make it their own. Many served a turkey surrounded by the celebratory dishes of their own cultures. For Jews, the early 1900s invention of Crisco as a nondairy butter substitute allowed them to create a truly “American” Thanksgiving and dessert, without violating kosher rules against mixing meat and milk. The fact that most families celebrate at home allowed immigrants and their children to take part in the national culture, while still expressing their own. During my own New England childhood, an Indian neighbor had my mother’s fairly classic cranberry relish, and by the end of the weekend she’d worked out a cranberry chutney with Indian spices. When we had Thankgiving dinner with my parents’ friends the Stalzmans, who were Jewish, matzah ball soup was the opening course. At times, the idea of the Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower has been used to exclude – to imply that only Americans whose literal ancestors came over on the ship , and other white Protestants like them, truly belong. Yet on the holiday in their memory, generations of new Americans affirmed that they, too, belonged. Samira Mehta , Professor of Women and Gender Studies & Jewish Studies, University of Colorado Boulder This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: America’s missile stockpiles will take years to rebuild after Iran—and a watchdog warns the Pentagon has a blind spot
summary: The Navy bought an average of 86 Tomahawks a year for a decade, then fired more than 1,000 at Iran. A new GAO report finds no single Pentagon office owns the fix.
content: Over the past decade, the U.S. military bought an average of 86 Tomahawk cruise missiles a year. In the war with Iran, it has fired more than 1,000, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). That math explains why stockpiles of two of America’s most relied-upon weapons, the Tomahawk and the Patriot air-defense interceptor, will take years to refill. Under current Pentagon delivery projections, CSIS estimates the Tomahawks fired at Iran won’t be fully replaced until late 2030. The Army’s 3,203 Patriot interceptors requested for fiscal 2027 aren’t projected to start arriving until May 2029. A new watchdog report says the Pentagon isn’t organized to close that gap. In “DOD Munitions: Planning and Leadership Needed to Address Persistent Shortages,” released Nov. 19, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the Defense Department has no overarching plan linking munitions production and funding to its requirements, and no office with the authority to carry one out. Fortune reported on the GAO’s findings this week. Why Tomahawks and Patriots are so hard to replace Both weapons are Cold War designs. The National Air and Space Museum says Tomahawks were developed in the late 1970s and became fully operational in the early 1980s. The Patriot’s precursors date to the mid-1960s, and systems comparable to today’s arrived in the early 1980s, per CSIS. The Tomahawk is a ship- and submarine-launched cruise missile with a range of roughly 1,000 miles. The Patriot is a defensive system that can intercept incoming missiles, drones, and manned aircraft, per Raytheon. Besides the U.S., four allies field Tomahawks: the U.K., Australia, the Netherlands, and Japan. Raytheon, a unit of RTX , makes every Tomahawk in the U.S., and RTX is No. 49 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . The U.S. and 18 other countries operate the Patriot, and several other nations, including Germany and Japan, also manufacture Patriot systems. The Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel launched on Feb. 28, drew both stockpiles down fast. U.S. destroyers and submarines have fired about a third of the prewar Tomahawk inventory, and about two-thirds of the prewar Patriot interceptor inventory has been expended against Iranian ballistic missiles, according to an updated CSIS analysis . Transfers to Ukraine had already thinned Patriot stocks. Production hasn’t kept pace because orders didn’t. Recent Tomahawk output has run below 200 missiles a year, though Raytheon aims for capacity of more than 1,000, CSIS found. Lockheed Martin , which builds the Patriot’s PAC-3 MSE interceptor, makes about 600 a year and is targeting 2,000 a year by 2030. New interceptors will be spoken for quickly. CSIS estimates about 1,600 were already in the allied backlog before the war, and coalition partners that fired their own Patriots during the Iran war have since bought more. What the GAO found, and what it couldn’t say The GAO’s public report doesn’t say which munitions are short. It is a version of a classified report issued Sept. 24, and the Pentagon deemed inventory trends and persistent shortfalls too sensitive to release. The public version lays out a management problem. “DOD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” the auditors wrote. “According to DOD officials, in lieu of a plan, DOD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.” The report cites the Army’s push to produce more 155-millimeter artillery shells, which addressed shortages worsened by U.S. support to allies but “was not driven by DOD’s total munitions requirement.” Without a plan that sets long-term goals and metrics, the GAO warned, the Pentagon risks persistently low inventories, or “investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.” Leadership is spread thin. Each service manages its own stockpile; for example, the Navy’s Tomahawk Weapon System Program Office oversees the Navy’s inventory. A Munitions Acceleration Council created in July 2025 to speed missile production still had no formal signed charter as of November 2026, a senior Pentagon official told the GAO. Service officials told auditors that without a dedicated leadership office, “it may be difficult to realize progress in addressing munitions shortages at any level.” The GAO made four recommendations, including that the Pentagon write an overarching munitions plan and name an office with the authority to carry it out. The department generally concurred. The stakes are financial and military. A plan could guide how the Pentagon spends at least $25 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for munitions, the GAO noted. Experts split on whether planning or capacity is the real bottleneck “The GAO findings illustrate what everyone can see with their own eyes,” Michael Horowitz, senior fellow for technology and innovation and director of the Defense and National Security Program at the Council on Foreign Relations, tells Fortune . His prescription is to change what the Pentagon buys. “The single most important thing the Pentagon needs to do is continue ramping investments in precise mass systems like inexpensive cruise missiles and long-range, one-way attack drones,” Horowitz says, “because the supply chains and production processes will be easier. This will build resiliency and redundancy into the system.” Michael O’Hanlon, director of foreign policy research and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, puts less weight on the missing plan. “I don’t see it quite this way,” he tells Fortune . “DoD is scurrying constantly to work with industry to scale up production of key munitions. The issue is less the absence of a single formal plan on paper and much more physical constraints limiting capacity. A better plan might help, but it’s not the core issue or driver.” CSIS reached a similar conclusion in May: With bipartisan support in Congress for munitions funding, the constraint is no longer money but the time it takes to expand capacity and build complex weapons. Elaine McCusker, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former acting undersecretary of defense (comptroller), sees both forces at work. Asked about the main obstacles to replenishment, among them factory capacity, supply chains and critical materials, contracting, and unpredictable demand, she added one more. “I would add workforce to that, which is also negatively impacted by the ups and downs of the budget and requirements demand,” McCusker says. “I think two things drive the time it takes to rebuild the stockpile: predictable resourcing to make the most of, and expand, the production capacity of current manufacturing and supply chains and the urgency placed on developing, testing and producing entirely new munitions — and interceptor — solutions.” Her fix starts with the budget. “Fully fund the military budget on time each fiscal year,” she says. “Fund full automation of the Pentagon inventory, parts, and supply system, which is a key component of solving material weaknesses for the department to pass a full financial statement audit, but more importantly, as we see with munitions, it is necessary for readiness and munitions stockpile planning.” What to watch The next test is the fiscal 2027 budget. The administration has requested $1.5 trillion for defense, including 785 Tomahawks and 3,203 Patriot interceptors, though CSIS doubts Congress will pass the full request. Also watch whether the Pentagon names an office to own the munitions problem, as the GAO recommended. Even if Congress funds every missile on time, the timeline is long. The first Tomahawks from the 2027 order aren’t projected to reach U.S. inventories until March 2030, after nearly three years of production lead time. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
